name: UI libraries
summary: Reusable interface parts: styled components you drop in and theme, or headless ones that handle state, keyboard and accessibility while you write the markup and styles.
howItWorks: Most apps need the same parts: buttons, dialogs, menus, comboboxes, date pickers, data tables. Each part has two layers. The behaviour layer holds state (is the menu open, which row is selected, how the rows are sorted) and the interaction rules, such as the roles and keys the W3C’s ARIA Authoring Practices Guide sets out for each widget: in a combobox, Down Arrow moves into the popup and Escape closes it. The presentation layer is the markup and CSS. A component library ships both layers and implements one design system: Material UI renders Google’s Material Design, and you adjust it through a theme object (colours, spacing, shape) rather than rewriting its CSS. A headless library ships only the behaviour. TanStack Table hands you header groups and sorted rows and renders nothing; Radix Primitives, Headless UI, React Aria and Base UI render unstyled, accessible parts that you style with Tailwind, CSS Modules or plain CSS. A third route, shadcn/ui, copies styled component source into your repository instead of installing it as a package, with headless parts underneath. The trade is speed against control: a component library looks finished on day one but fights a design that differs from its own, while a headless one fits any design and leaves every element and style to you.
analogy: Furniture. A component library is a showroom set: sofa, table and chairs that match and arrive assembled, in the maker’s style. A headless library is the hardware: hinges, drawer runners and locks that work smoothly, fitted into cabinets you design yourself.
useWhen: Internal tools and admin screens where shipping fast matters more than a distinctive look: a component library
A product with its own design system: build it on headless parts so you own the markup and styles
Widgets whose keyboard and screen reader behaviour is easy to get wrong by hand, such as comboboxes, menus, dialogs and data grids
One behaviour across several frameworks: TanStack Table’s core has adapters for React, Vue, Solid, Svelte, Angular and five more
avoidWhen: Restyling a component library far away from its design system; MUI’s own team writes that Material UI “can become unwieldy” when a design diverges significantly
A quick prototype on a headless library: you write and style every element yourself
Mixing several component libraries in one app; shadcn/ui’s docs describe the usual result as wrapped components, style workarounds and incompatible APIs
example: A team needs an orders table with sorting, filtering and pagination. With a component library’s data grid they pass `rows` and `columns` and have a finished grid in an afternoon, though in MUI X multi-column sorting and column pinning sit in the paid Pro package and row grouping in Premium. With TanStack Table they register the sorting, filtering and pagination features, then render their own `<table>` with the design system’s classes. It takes more code, but the table matches every other screen, and the same sorted rows can drive a card list on mobile.

source: type Order = { id: string; customer: string; total: number }
// the headless library holds the state and the sorting logic
const table = constructTable({ features, columns, data })
// what a click on the “Total” header would call
// the markup is yours: here, plain text lines instead of <tr> elements

kinds.name: Component libraries
kinds.summary: Styled, ready-made components that implement one design system, which you theme rather than build.
body: A component library ships finished components: markup, styles, behaviour and a theme. Material UI implements Google’s Material Design (version 2) for React. You install `@mui/material` together with Emotion, its default styling engine, then change colours, typography, spacing and shapes in a theme object, or a single element through the `sx` prop. Bootstrap does the same in CSS and HTML: it served as Twitter’s style guide for internal tools for more than a year before its public release in August 2011.

Pick one when the design system it implements is close enough to yours, or when looks matter less than speed, as in internal tools and admin screens. The cost shows when your design diverges: overrides component by component, extra CSS specificity for states such as disabled or focused, and breaking changes at each major version. Some libraries are open core: Material UI is MIT-licensed, while advanced data grid features in MUI X need a paid licence.

kinds.name: Headless libraries
kinds.summary: State, logic and accessible behaviour for UI elements with no markup or styles of their own; you render and style everything.
body: A headless library supplies the hard part of a widget and leaves the rendering to you. TanStack Table defines headless UI as libraries that provide “the logic, state, processing, and APIs for UI elements and interactions” but no markup, styles or pre-built implementations. A table instance gives you header groups and sorted, filtered rows; your code turns them into a `<table>`, a card list or anything else, with any CSS or component library.

Others ship unstyled components that already render accessible markup. Radix Primitives and Base UI follow the WAI-ARIA design patterns, and Radix takes care of roles, focus management and keyboard navigation; Headless UI from Tailwind Labs is “completely unstyled, fully accessible”, designed for Tailwind CSS. Base UI, from people behind Radix, Material UI and Floating UI, reached 1.0 in December 2025. shadcn/ui builds on such primitives and copies its styled layer into your repository.
Pick headless when you have your own design system, or need the same behaviour in several frameworks. Expect to write more code: every element and every style is yours.

story: Bootstrap set the pattern for component libraries. Two Twitter employees (@mdo and @fat) built it in mid-2010 as Twitter Blueprint, and it served as the company’s style guide for internal tools for over a year before its public release on 19 August 2011. In 2014 Material UI started as a React implementation of Google’s Material Design guidelines. Both gave teams one design language with ready-made parts, and both grew into some of the most widely used front-end projects.

Ready-made parts are hard to bend. In one MUI developer survey, five times as many developers as the year before were struggling to customize the components, and customization became the focus of Material UI v5. In June 2018 Merrick Christensen had described the other answer: a headless user interface component “offers maximum visual flexibility by providing no interface”. React Table v7 (March 2020) was rebuilt on that idea as a hooks-only utility that renders nothing.

Headless libraries for accessible widgets followed: Radix Primitives, Headless UI, React Aria, and in 2022 MUI Base (now Base UI), MUI’s headless alternative to its own library. shadcn/ui then combined the two models by copying styled component source, built on headless parts, into each project, citing AI models that read and improve the code as one more reason to own it.

choices.why: React Table v7’s release notes gave three reasons: the look of a table belongs to the app, dropping UI options removes a huge API surface to maintain, and an app can extend a design the library never imagined.

The W3C’s Authoring Practices Guide documents roles, states and keyboard rules for widgets such as comboboxes and menus. Libraries that implement them once save every app from re-deriving focus management and key handling.

choices.choice: A theme object instead of editing CSS
choices.why: Material UI v1 moved from inline styles, which lacked media queries and pseudo-selectors, to CSS-in-JS with a JavaScript theme holding the palette, typography and breakpoints, so a brand could be applied in one place.
shadcn/ui argues that installed libraries end in wrappers and style workarounds, so it hands you the component code to edit directly while the headless layer underneath still updates as a dependency.
